On the right, layout_forceatlas2(seed=1) pulls each triangle together and pushes the triangles apart, so they sit as three separate clusters linked in a ring." width="100%"} ForceAtlas2 (Jacomy, Venturini, Heymann & Bastian, 2014) gives every node a mass of its degree plus one. Every pair of nodes repels with force `scaling_ratio * m_i * m_j / d`, so hubs push others away hard; every edge attracts its ends with force `w * d`; and gravity pulls every node toward the centroid with force `gravity * m`, so disconnected pieces don't fly off. Steps adapt as the run goes: nodes whose force keeps swinging back and forth move less, nodes pulled steadily one way move more, and a global speed rises or falls with how much the whole layout swings. The result is centered and scaled so the largest coordinate is `scale=`. The options are the ones in Gephi: - `linlog=True` uses the weaker attraction `w * log(1 + d)`, which separates clusters more sharply (Noack's LinLog energy); - `dissuade_hubs=True` divides each node's attraction by its mass, pushing hubs toward the edge of their cluster and authorities toward the center; - `strong_gravity=True` makes gravity grow with distance, `gravity * m * d`, for a more compact picture; - `node_size=` turns on overlap prevention: distances are measured between node borders, overlapping nodes repel strongly and stop attracting. Each iteration costs `O(n^2)` (run in parallel on larger graphs; Gephi uses a Barnes-Hut approximation instead). Edge direction is ignored and parallel edges add their weights. NetworkX's `forceatlas2_layout()` takes the same parameters (its `distributed_action=` is `dissuade_hubs=` here), but it measures swing from positions rather than successive forces, and it returns unscaled coordinates; the update here follows the paper and Gephi. Positions are stored as `[x, y]` lists in the `attr_name=` node attribute; see `layout_circular()`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [max_iter]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [int]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[100]{.dv}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Number of iterations. The run stops sooner if the layout stops moving. Default is `100`. [jitter_tolerance]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : How much swinging is tolerated: higher values allow faster, less precise convergence. Default is `1.0`. [scaling_ratio]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[2.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Strength of the repulsion; higher values spread the layout out. Default is `2.0`. [gravity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[1.0]{.fl}]{.doc-parameter-default} : Strength of the pull toward the centroid. Default is `1.0`. [strong_gravity]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, gravity grows with distance from the centroid. Default is `False`. [linlog]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, use logarithmic attraction (LinLog mode). Default is `False`. If `return_dict=` is `False` (default): returns self for method chaining. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `jitter_tolerance=` or `scaling_ratio=` is not positive, `gravity=` is negative, a mass is not positive or a size is negative, an initial position is not a pair of finite numbers, `weighted=True` and an edge weight is negative, or `scale=` or `center=` is invalid. ::: ## See Also {.doc-see-also} [](`~layout_spring`) : Place nodes with a force-directed spring model. [](`~cmty_louvain`) : Find communities with the Louvain method. [](`~layout_arf`) : Place nodes with attractive and repulsive forces. ## Examples {.doc-examples} ForceAtlas2 is a force-directed layout made for social networks. Its LinLog mode weakens the attraction between joined nodes, which pulls communities apart. ### Communities of dolphins Bottlenose dolphins in a New Zealand fjord, joined when two were often seen together, colored by their Louvain communities. The default mode on the left already groups them. LinLog on the right pulls the communities further apart and stretches the edges between them: ::: {layout-ncol="2"} ::: {#45179258 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec dolphins = ec.dolphins().cmty_louvain(attr_name="community") dolphins.layout_forceatlas2(seed=4).plot( layout="pos", color_by="community", show_labels=False, width=360, height=360, legend=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: {#e10d137d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} dolphins.layout_forceatlas2(linlog=True, seed=4).plot( layout="pos", color_by="community", show_labels=False, width=360, height=360, legend=False, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: The result depends on `seed=`. `max_iter=` trades time for a more settled layout. [Layouts](../user-guide/layouts.qmd#force-directed-layouts) compares the four force-directed layouts on the dolphin network, and shows how `linlog=True` separates its communities.
